objectives: Define specialisation, competence and scope, and say how knowing a field well differs from being able to judge it from outside.
Describe what specialisation gives a person: speed, a shared vocabulary, a memory of past cases, and the confidence to say no.
Explain why a strong habit of thinking becomes a blind spot outside the field that trained it.
Compare the blind spot of five fields: engineering, finance, law, medicine, and sales or operations.
Follow six steps to check the blind spot of your own field before a decision goes out.
Name the three situations where a blind spot turns into damage: one field in the room, one reader, and the author as the checker.
Use ready sentences to ask another field for its view without offending the expert.

sections.body:
**Specialisation** is the work of knowing one field deeply and going deeper instead of going wide. A **specialist** is a person whose work is in one field and who is trusted to judge work in that field: to read a drawing, a contract, a ledger or a patient and to say what is wrong with it. That trust is earned. It comes from years of cases, from mistakes seen and from vocabulary learned from other people who did the same work.

Two words sit next to it and are often mixed up. **Competence** is the ability to do a piece of work well, and it belongs to the person. **Scope** is the area that a person, a document or a decision covers, and it belongs to the work. A person can have high competence and a narrow scope: excellent with a motor, with no idea about the contract that pays for it. A person can also have a wide scope and thin competence: many subjects, none of them carried deep enough to be trusted on their own.

The line that matters at work runs between knowing a field and judging it from outside. A person who knows a field well can read a document from another field and still get it wrong, and can do it quickly. **Blind spot** is the name for that failure: the part of the situation the person cannot see well, because the habits of one field have trained the eyes to look in one direction. The failure is not a lack of intelligence and it is not laziness. It is a strong model of the world being used where a different model is needed.

This article is about that line. It gives you the words for the two sides of it, a way to check your own blind spot before a decision goes out, and the sentences that let you ask another field for its view without turning the request into an accusation.
examples: She is the specialist for the pump, so she read the report in ten minutes.
My competence is in the numbers; the scope of this decision is much wider.
Knowing a field well is not the same as being able to judge it from outside.
His blind spot is the customer: the figure was right and nobody asked who was waiting.
sections.heading: What specialisation is, and what it puts out of sight

terms.example: Specialisation is why the same engineer finds a fault in ten minutes that takes another person a day.
terms.gloss: The work of knowing one field deeply instead of many fields broadly.

terms.gloss: A person whose work is in one field and who is trusted to judge work in that field.

terms.example: The scope of this decision covers the money, the contract and the customer.
terms.gloss: The area of work that a person, a document or a decision covers.

terms.example: His competence is in the numbers; the rest of the project is not his field.
terms.gloss: The ability to do a piece of work well.

terms.example: Her blind spot is the customer: the figure was right and nobody asked who was waiting for the machine.

sections.body:
The gains of specialisation are real, and it is worth saying so plainly before the costs. A specialist reads a familiar document faster than anybody else in the room, because the document is mostly a repetition of things already known. An engineer sees the tolerance in a drawing in one pass. A doctor sees the symptom in the first sentence of a note. An accountant sees the wrong number in a table without going looking for it.

A field also has a shared vocabulary. Inside it, people use the same words for the same things, and the words are enough. *That bearing is out of tolerance* means one thing in the workshop, and everybody in the workshop knows it. The vocabulary is a shared tool: it saves the time that explanation would cost. It is also the place where the field closes around itself, because a word that is obvious inside the field says almost nothing outside it.

Specialists also carry a memory of the cases that came before. The experienced engineer has seen this crack, this leak and this failure before, and the memory is faster than any calculation. That is why a good specialist refuses a design that looks correct on paper. They are not being difficult. They are reading a pattern.

And a specialist has the confidence to say no. The **judgement** to stop work, to reject a part, to refuse a claim. That confidence is worth money, and it is the reason employers pay for it. All four gains come from the same place: years of practice in one field. That is also where the cost comes from.
examples: Let the specialist read it first; it will take two minutes instead of two hours.
He said no to the part, and he was right: he had seen that failure before.
We are buying that judgement, so let us use it instead of guessing.
sections.heading: What specialisation gives, and why the world pays for it

terms.example: The judgement to stop the line is part of what the company pays for.
terms.gloss: The ability to form an opinion from experience and to defend it.

sections.body:
Outside the field, the same person reads a document quickly and reads it wrongly. The accountant who knows the ledger perfectly sees a page of figures and never sees the customer who will cancel the order. The engineer who knows the machine perfectly sees a contract and reads only the technical clauses, and does not notice the termination clause. The lawyer who knows the law perfectly reads a maintenance report and sees no duty of care in it at all. Each of them is right inside the field and wrong outside it, and the two facts sit together.

The reason is that a strong habit of thinking becomes a blinder. The habits of one field are shortcuts, and they are good shortcuts inside the field. The accountant is trained to read a number as a fact to be traced, not as a complaint to be answered. The engineer is trained to read a sentence as a specification to be built, not as a promise to be kept. **Bias** is the name for this leaning of the mind: it is not a prejudice about people, it is a habit of attention that points one way.

This is why the mistake is not stupidity. The mind does not start from nothing on every document. It starts from the model it knows and fits the new material into it. A model that has worked for fifteen years is very hard to switch off, and there is no switch. The mind reads the contract as a machine, or the machine as a contract, because that is the shape it already knows.

Every plan rests on an **assumption**: something the plan takes as true without checking it. Inside a field the assumptions are shared and mostly correct, so nobody writes them down. Outside it the same assumptions are carried over, and there they are often wrong. The way to find them is not to work harder inside the field. It is to ask somebody who does not work in it.
examples: He read the contract as a specification and missed the clause that ends the contract.
The bias is not against the customer; it is away from the customer.
State the assumptions, because the other field will not supply them for you.
sections.heading: What specialisation takes away: the blind spot outside the field

terms.example: The bias is not against the customer; it is away from the customer.
terms.gloss: A habit of attention that leans one way, often without the person noticing.

terms.example: The hidden assumption is that the machine will be ready on the first day.
terms.gloss: Something a plan takes as true without checking it.

sections.body:
Each row names one field, what the years of practice in that field sharpen, what those same years put out of sight, and the question to ask somebody from outside. The four columns answer four different questions, and the fourth one is the practical one.

Read the rows as a description of a field, never as a ranking of people. A field is not better or worse than another field. Each one was built to solve a particular problem, and each one leaves something outside the frame that it was never asked to cover.
examples: Ask the person who carries the consequence what this failure costs them.
Give the team the field they never look at, not the field they are best at.
This row describes a field, not the people who work in it.
sections.heading: The blind spot of each field

rows: Engineering is the field that builds and repairs machines.
It sharpens the reading of machines, materials and drawings.
It hides the customer, the contract and the cost of a delay.
Ask the person who carries the consequence what this failure costs them.
Finance is the field that plans and follows the money.
It sharpens the reading of money, risk and the shape of a number.
It hides the customer behind the number and the work behind the budget.
Ask the people doing the work what the budget makes impossible.
Law is the field that sets out rights and duties.
It sharpens the reading of rights, duties and the exact words of a clause.
It hides the machine and the work, and how they behave in service.
Ask the technician what the machine really does once it is running.
Medicine is the field that treats the sick and the injured.
It sharpens the reading of symptoms, results and the pattern of a case.
It hides the life of the patient outside the clinic.
Ask the nurse or the family what the day looks like at home.
Sales and operations are the fields that bring the work and the customer together.
They sharpen the reading of customers, targets and the way work moves.
They hide the cost of a promise and the load it puts on the team.
Ask the team that carries the work what the promise costs them.

terms.example: His field is tax, so read the customs part with somebody else.
terms.gloss: An area of work that a person knows well enough to work in.

sections.body:
The check takes half an hour and it is done on one real decision, not on a theory. The six steps are in order. The first two find the fields that your own field is hiding from you, the middle two pull the numbers and the motives out of the other field, and the last two put the result in writing where somebody else can check it.

Two rules keep this honest. Use a decision that is real and that has not gone out yet, because a decision that has already gone out cannot be checked. And ask a person, not a document: a document answers the question you asked it, and a person answers the one you did not think of.
examples: Write the decision in one line, then list every field it touches.
Ask one person from another field what my plan takes for granted.
Here is what I did not understand, in writing. Is it right, and what did I leave out?
sections.heading: How to check your own blind spot in six steps
steps: Name the decision and the fields it touches. Write the decision in one line, the way it will be written when it is signed. Then write down every field it depends on: the money, the law, the machine, the customer, the people who will do the work. A decision that touches one field has one blind spot to look for. A decision that touches three has three.

Ask somebody from another field what your plan assumes. Give that person one sentence about the plan and one question: what does this plan take for granted? Write the answers down without arguing with them. The value of the answer is in what you did not expect to hear.

Look for the number your field never looks at. Every field watches one measure closely and ignores the others. The accountant watches the cost and not the churn. The engineer watches the cycle time and not the complaint. The seller watches the revenue and not the support tickets. Ask somebody who keeps the ignored measure for its last value.

Ask what the other side is paid for. In every field the other side has an income, and the income says what they are paid to notice. The support team is paid to close tickets, so tickets are what they watch. The lawyer is paid to protect the company from claims, so claims are what they look for. Ask what the other side is paid for, and expect the answer to name what they do not worry about.

Read the document of the other field, even badly. Read the contract if you are not a lawyer, the drawing if you are not an engineer, the ledger if you are not an accountant. You will read it badly, and that is the point: you will see the parts your own field never explains and never asks about. Mark the words you do not understand.

Write down what you did not understand and ask. Put the list in writing and send it to one person in the other field with one question: is this right, and what have I left out? This is the **verification** step of the whole routine. A plan that has been checked by somebody who works in the other field is not perfect, but it is not blind either.

terms.example: Verification of the cost is done by finance, not by the person who wrote the estimate.
terms.gloss: The checking of a thing against a source before it is trusted.

sections.body:
The blind spot becomes dangerous in three situations, and all three are common. The first is a decision that crosses two fields when only one field is in the room. An engineer and a lawyer are needed to read a supply contract, and the meeting has one of them. The second is when the expert is also the only reader: one person reads the document and nobody else sees it, so there is no second pair of eyes at all. The third is when the plan is checked by the person who wrote it. Self-checking feels thorough, and it only confirms what the writer already had in mind.

A second pair of eyes from another field is not a criticism of the expert. It is the cheapest insurance in the room. The expert is usually right inside the field, and the reader from outside is usually wrong about the details. That is exactly why the two together are better than either one alone: each one sees the part the other one cannot.

A **second opinion** is the judgement of a second person, asked because the first one may not see everything. Two rules keep it practical. Ask the question in the language of the other field, and give the person time to read the document before the meeting. A second opinion given in five minutes from a document nobody read is worth very little.
examples: Before we sign, I want a second opinion from somebody outside this field.
The plan was checked by the person who wrote it, so nothing was really checked.
This is not a criticism of the expert; it is the cheapest insurance in the room.
sections.heading: Where the blind spot turns dangerous

terms.example: Before we sign, I would like a second opinion from somebody outside this field.
terms.gloss: The judgement of a second person, asked because the first one may not see everything.

sections.body:
These are the sentences for a review, a meeting or a written plan. They ask another field for its view, and they do it without telling the expert that the expert is wrong. The first three ask a question. The next four are for the moment when you have to say that the plan is not ready yet.

One rule holds all of them together: ask about the plan, not about the person. *What does this plan take for granted?* is a question about the work. *You have not thought about this* is a statement about the person, and it ends the conversation. Say what you cannot see, ask what the other field would see, and let the expert answer.
examples: You know this field better than I do. What does my plan take for granted?
What would you check in this document that I would not think to check?
My plan is written in the language of my field; tell me what it leaves out.
You are right inside your field, and I need a view from outside it.
Before this goes out, I would like a second opinion from somebody in the other field.
Here is what I did not understand, in writing. Is it right, and what have I left out?
The number is right. What I cannot see from here is what it does to the customer.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
A team can defend against the blind spot in four ways. The first is to put different fields at the same table. A decision that one field alone can make is a decision that will be made with one blind spot. When the engineer, the lawyer and the person from operations are in the same room, each of them sees the part the others do not, and the decision is better for it.

The second way is to give somebody the job of asking the question from outside. Some teams appoint a person whose only task in a decision meeting is to ask what the plan takes for granted, and which field is missing from the room. That person does not have to be the best at anything. They have to stand outside the field the rest of the room is standing in.

The third way is a written decision that says where each assumption comes from. A short note under every assumption: the delivery date comes from production, the penalty comes from legal, the cost comes from finance. When every assumption carries the name of its field, a missing field becomes visible on the page, and the reader can see which part nobody owns.

The fourth way is to check the **handover**. Every handover of work is a handover between fields, and it is where a blind spot is passed on silently. A **generalist** is a person who works across several fields and can explain one of them to another, and the handover is the moment that person earns their place: they ask what the person leaving understood, and what they assumed. A strong expert working alone cannot do any of these four things, because there is nobody in the room to see what the expert cannot see.
examples: Put the engineer, the lawyer and operations in the same room for this decision.
Which field is missing from this room?
Under every assumption, write the field it comes from.
At the handover, ask what the other side assumed.
sections.heading: How a team defends against it

terms.example: At the handover she asked what the customer had actually agreed to.
terms.gloss: The passing of work from one person to another.

terms.example: The generalist on the team translated the tax rule into plain words.
terms.gloss: A person who works across several fields and can explain one of them to another.

item.summary: A deep specialist reads a document from another field quickly and reads it wrongly, and the mistake is not stupidity. After reading this you can name what specialisation sharpens and what it hides, find the blind spot of your own field, run a six-step check on a decision that crosses two fields, and ask another field for its view without offending anybody.
item.title: Specialisation and the Blind Spot: How the Best in One Field Misjudges Another
